case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Second Amendment permits Congress to categorically prohibit firearm possession by a person who is an “unlawful user of or addicted to” controlled substances—even when the person is not shown to be intoxicated at the moment of possession—as applied to Ali Danial Hemani.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) (prohibiting firearm possession by anyone who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance”), evaluated under the Second Amendment framework articulated in New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that § 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied because history and tradition support disarming people whose ongoing condition or status makes firearm possession especially dangerous, and modern unlawful drug use is sufficiently analogous to historically regulated states like intoxication and other conditions tied to impaired judgment and heightened risk. The government emphasizes that the Fifth Circuit’s decision effectively invalidates most real-world applications of § 922(g)(3), creates (and deepens) a circuit split, and threatens an important, frequently used federal public-safety statute. It contends Bruen does not require a one-to-one historical twin; it requires a relevantly similar analogue, and longstanding traditions of restricting weapons from dangerous or impaired persons justify § 922(g)(3) for active, habitual unlawful users.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Hemani argues § 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied because the Second Amendment protects his possession absent proof he was intoxicated or otherwise dangerous at the time he possessed the firearm, and because the government cannot identify a sufficiently similar historical tradition of disarming ordinary citizens based on drug use status alone. He maintains Bruen demands a close historical fit and that the best historical analogues (such as temporary intoxication restrictions) do not support a broad, ongoing prohibition keyed to being an unlawful user, as opposed to being actively impaired while armed. He further defends the Fifth Circuit’s conclusion that § 922(g)(3) sweeps too broadly by disarming people without individualized proof of dangerousness or contemporaneous impairment.
key_precedents: New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen
United States v. Harris (3d Cir. 2025) (as referenced in petitioner’s reply)
United States v. Hill (E.D. Va. 2023), aff’d (4th Cir. 2025), cert. denied (2025) (as referenced in the materials)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point—that the best Founding-era analogues are temporary intoxication restrictions and individualized surety measures, not an ongoing status-based ban—remains the central overbreadth concern. But Rahimi’s clarification of Bruen matters: the government need not find a historical twin, and those intoxication and preventive-justice traditions can support a comparably preventive restriction where the disqualifying condition is current and ongoing, not remote. I agree with Justice Gorsuch that we cannot "rewrite" § 922(g)(3), yet we can decide narrowly on an as-applied record by insisting on a meaningful temporal nexus to active, habitual unlawful use, which keeps the statute’s burden and justification closer to the historical model than the Fifth Circuit’s moment-of-possession intoxication requirement. On minimalist, institution-preserving grounds, I would reverse without endorsing the statute’s outermost applications based on stale evidence.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s reliance on Rahimi’s “why/how” analogical framework does not cure the government’s failure to identify a founding-era tradition of disarming people based on a continuing status of prior unlawful drug use untethered to contemporaneous impairment or an individualized judicial finding of dangerousness. The surety and other preventive-justice measures they invoke were targeted, adjudicative, and conditional—imposing tailored restraints after a showing of specific threat—unlike § 922(g)(3)’s categorical criminal ban that can be triggered by stale evidence without any present-risk determination. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett’s proposed “as-applied” narrowing to “active, habitual” users asks the Court to supply limiting principles not found in the statute’s text, and Bruen’s history test cannot be satisfied by rewriting modern law to resemble a tradition the government has not shown. Rahimi confirms we need not find a “historical twin,” but it still demands a relevant analogue; extending moment-of-intoxication carry restrictions into an indefinite possession disqualification exceeds that demonstrated historical boundary.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest objection: the Founding-era analogues most clearly reached carrying while actually intoxicated or imposed individualized surety-like conditions, not a categorical, ongoing disarmament keyed to “status” that might be proved by stale evidence. But Rahimi, as the Chief Justice emphasizes, confirms Bruen does not demand a historical twin; it asks whether the modern law addresses a comparable danger in a comparably preventive way, and disarming confirmed current unlawful users—understood with a real temporal nexus to active, ongoing use—fits within the tradition of risk-management restrictions aimed at impaired self-control. I agree with Justice Gorsuch that we cannot “rewrite” the statute, yet requiring proof of intoxication at the precise moment of possession would itself effectively constitutionalize an atextual limitation and largely nullify § 922(g)(3)’s core application to habitual users. The proper narrowing is as-applied: where the government proves ongoing, contemporaneous unlawful use (not remote or episodic conduct), the burden and justification are close enough to historical intoxication and preventive-justice measures to sustain the statute under Bruen/Rahimi.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest objection—that Founding-era intoxication regulations were temporary and tied to contemporaneous impairment, making § 922(g)(3) an impermissible status-based disarmament—has force, but it overreads Bruen’s analogue requirement. As the Chief Justice and Justice Alito emphasize through Rahimi, the inquiry is whether the law addresses a comparable danger in a comparably preventive way; a prohibition limited to proven, active, ongoing unlawful use reasonably functions as a proxy for recurring impairment and heightened risk, and we should not constitutionalize a moment-of-possession intoxication requirement that would largely nullify Congress’s protective judgment. I agree with Justice Gorsuch that stale-evidence applications raise serious concerns, but those are best handled by a tight as-applied temporal-nexus requirement rather than by invalidating the statute’s core coverage of current habitual users. On my pragmatic, real-world impacts approach, the respondent’s theory would most harm communities already burdened by gun violence by making enforcement nearly impossible against the very cases presenting the greatest continuing risk.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s best point is that the historical analogues look temporary and individualized, while § 922(g)(3) can be status-like and proved with stale evidence—so we cannot “rewrite” the statute to save it. But Rahimi, as the Chief emphasizes, makes clear Bruen’s inquiry is not a hunt for a historical twin; it asks whether the modern law addresses a comparable danger in a comparably preventive way, and a properly cabined application to active, ongoing unlawful users (with a real temporal nexus) matches the why/how of intoxication and preventive-justice traditions better than the Fifth Circuit’s near-instant-intoxication requirement. I take Justice Thomas’s concern seriously that surety was judicially supervised, but that goes to outer-bound applications untethered to present risk, not to Hemani’s kind of contemporaneous habitual use where the statute’s burden and justification align with the historical model. On a pragmatic textualist view, the limiting principle comes from the term “user” and ordinary temporal usage—policing administrability and overbreadth as applied—rather than constitutionalizing an enforcement-nullifying moment-of-possession rule.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed as-applied narrowing and Justice Alito’s reliance on Rahimi correctly stress that Bruen does not require a “historical twin,” but Rahimi’s why/how inquiry still demands a genuinely comparable burden and mechanism. The historical candidates they invoke—intoxication restrictions and surety-style preventive-justice measures—were typically temporary, tied to contemporaneous conduct or individualized judicial findings of threat, and did not impose a categorical, ongoing criminal disarmament keyed to a status that can be proved by noncontemporaneous use. I cannot adopt Justice Kagan’s suggestion to cabin the statute to “active, habitual” users as a saving construction where the statutory text and typical enforcement permit materially broader applications; doing so would rewrite Congress’s work and dilute Bruen by extending analogues beyond their demonstrated bounds. Where the government’s best analogues fall short in a criminal prohibition, separation-of-powers principles and the rule of lenity counsel resolving the mismatch against the government rather than fashioning a judicially invented temporality requirement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right to press the temporal mismatch: many historical intoxication rules were keyed to contemporaneous impairment, and § 922(g)(3) can be proved with evidence that is arguably stale. But as the Chief Justice notes, Rahimi reiterates Bruen’s “relevantly similar” inquiry focuses on comparable risk and comparable preventive burden, not a Founding-era “twin,” and that framework accommodates regulations aimed at ongoing dangerousness rather than only moment-of-possession intoxication. The proper institutional response is not to constitutionalize a strict contemporaneous-intoxication requirement (which would largely nullify the statute and is not demanded by history), but to enforce a tight as-applied temporal nexus so the prohibition operates as a proxy for current, regular unlawful use—bringing the law’s “why” and “how” closer to the historical tradition than the Fifth Circuit allowed. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity/separation-of-powers concern has force at the margins, but it does not defeat the statute’s core application where the record shows active, ongoing use and the burden is correspondingly limited in time and justification.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch raise the core historical objection: Founding-era regulations most directly addressed carrying or firing while actually intoxicated, and surety laws were individualized rather than categorical. But as the Chief Justice notes, Rahimi’s clarification of Bruen permits analogical reasoning focused on “why” and “how,” and a prohibition applied to proven, active unlawful use with a tight temporal nexus is relevantly similar to historical preventive measures aimed at forestalling armed misuse when self-control is predictably diminished. I agree with Justice Gorsuch that courts must not "rewrite" § 922(g)(3) into a moment-of-intoxication rule; instead, the limiting principle is an as-applied contemporaneity requirement that keeps the law’s burden and justification within the historical tradition while avoiding unconstitutional applications based on stale or episodic evidence. On a textualist view, that approach respects the statute’s words while ensuring the Second Amendment analysis turns on the record’s showing of ongoing unlawful use, not an atextual demand for proof of intoxication at the instant of possession.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point—that the historical record shows primarily temporary, contemporaneous-intoxication restrictions and individualized surety processes, not a categorical, status-based ban—squarely highlights the overbreadth risk of § 922(g)(3) as written. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito stress, Rahimi clarifies Bruen’s method: we look for a relevantly similar analogue in the law’s “why” and “how,” not a historical twin, and the tradition of restricting arms when a person’s present condition signals heightened risk supports disqualification tied to ongoing unlawful use. I agree with Justice Thomas that surety laws were more individualized, yet that cuts toward an as-applied narrowing principle rather than facial invalidation: requiring a meaningful temporal nexus and proof of current, regular unlawful use keeps the burden closer to the historically temporary, condition-linked restrictions while preserving administrability and the statute’s preventive function. Lenity, as Justice Gorsuch frames it, is not a substitute for the Second Amendment analogue inquiry; it can inform the statutory temporality question at the margins, but it does not erase the historical support for disarming those shown to be presently in a recurring impairment-risk category.

John Roberts.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s “relevantly similar” historical-analogue inquiry, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) can be upheld at least as applied to an active, ongoing unlawful user because the Nation has long accepted disarming or restricting arms for persons whose condition poses an enhanced risk—historically reflected in regulations tied to intoxication and other impairing conditions, even if not perfectly matched in duration. Rahimi confirms that Bruen does not demand a “historical twin” and permits analogical reasoning focused on why and how a regulation addresses danger; that approach supports targeting habitual unlawful drug use as a proxy for impaired judgment and heightened risk with firearms. Given the serious institutional and public-safety consequences of effectively nullifying a widely used federal prohibition, and consistent with judicial minimalism, the sound course is to reverse the Fifth Circuit and uphold § 922(g)(3) on narrow, as-applied grounds for confirmed, regular unlawful users rather than announce a sweeping rule about all status-based disarmament. This disposition respects precedent while avoiding unnecessary constitutional breadth and preserving Congress’s traditional latitude in firearm regulation within historical bounds.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text protects the right of “the people” to keep and bear arms, and under Bruen the Government must justify 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) by pointing to a well-established historical tradition of comparable firearm regulation. The historical evidence most closely resembles temporary restrictions on carrying while actually intoxicated, not a categorical, continuing disarmament based on the status of being an “unlawful user of or addicted to” a substance absent contemporaneous impairment or individualized dangerousness. Because § 922(g)(3) imposes an ongoing prohibition untethered to intoxication at the time of possession, it lacks a sufficiently analogous Founding- or Reconstruction-era tradition and therefore cannot be sustained as applied to Hemani under Bruen’s text-and-history test. Where precedent conflicts with the Constitution’s original public meaning, it must yield, and Bruen supplies the controlling framework here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied because the Nation has long accepted categorical firearm restrictions aimed at preventing gun misuse by persons whose ongoing condition makes armed possession especially risky. As Rahimi explains, Founding-era surety and other “preventive justice” measures targeted those with “probable ground to suspect of future misbehavior,” and Bruen does not demand a “historical twin” but only a relevant analogue with similar “why” and “how.” Section 922(g)(3) likewise addresses the heightened risk associated with habitual unlawful drug use and impaired judgment, and requiring proof of contemporaneous intoxication would undermine an important, frequently used public-safety statute in real-world enforcement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: As applied to Hemani, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) fits within a historically rooted tradition of temporarily disarming persons whose condition poses an elevated risk of violence or impaired judgment, and Bruen does not demand a “historical twin” so long as the modern regulation is relevantly similar in its why and how. Ongoing unlawful drug use is a continuing condition associated with impaired judgment and heightened danger, making § 922(g)(3)’s categorical bar a practical, administrable means of protecting the public—especially vulnerable communities disproportionately harmed by gun violence—without requiring the government to prove intoxication at the precise moment of possession. Under New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, the Fifth Circuit’s insistence on contemporaneous impairment applies the history-and-tradition inquiry at too narrow a level of generality and unduly hamstrings Congress’s ability to address modern public-safety risks. Given the statute’s limited reach to active “unlawful user[s]” or those “addicted to” controlled substances, § 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Applying Bruen, the question is whether § 922(g)(3)’s disarmament of active unlawful drug users is relevantly similar—in burden and justification—to historical regulations aimed at keeping firearms from persons whose impaired judgment or ongoing condition made armed carry especially risky. Although the historical record may not contain an exact “unlawful user” status category, Bruen does not demand a dead ringer; it asks for a well-matched analogue, and traditions of restricting arms use by the intoxicated and other dangerous/irresponsible persons support Congress’s judgment that ongoing unlawful use presents a comparable, recurring risk even when not proven intoxicated at the precise moment of possession. As applied to Hemani, § 922(g)(3) is also workable and administrable: it targets contemporaneous, habitual unlawful use (not remote, past use) and serves the statute’s public-safety purpose without requiring a moment-by-moment intoxication showing that would largely defeat the provision. This reading preserves statutory coherence across the federal disqualification scheme and respects Congress’s ability to address modern manifestations of historically recognized dangers consistent with Bruen’s analogical method.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s text presumptively covers Hemani’s possession, the burden shifts to the government to identify a relevantly similar historical analogue justifying § 922(g)(3)’s categorical, status-based disarmament. The best proffered analogues—Founding- and Reconstruction-era restrictions on carrying or using firearms while actively intoxicated—are materially narrower in both “why” and “how,” because they target contemporaneous impairment and typically operate temporarily rather than imposing an ongoing ban untethered to intoxication at the moment of possession. Section 922(g)(3), as implemented, can disarm a person based on past use (e.g., months-old evidence) without a showing of present impairment or individualized dangerousness, and that breadth lacks the historically grounded fit Bruen (as clarified by Rahimi’s “relevantly similar” requirement) demands. Any remaining ambiguity about extending historical intoxication regulations into an indefinite, status-based prohibition in a criminal statute should be resolved against the government under the rule of lenity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Bruen, the government must justify 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) by identifying a historical tradition of firearm regulation that is “relevantly similar” in purpose and burden, not a one-to-one historical twin. History and tradition support disarming or restricting arms from persons whose ongoing condition creates an elevated risk to public safety—especially where the restriction targets habitual, current unlawful use that is closely tied to impaired judgment and dangerous conduct, akin to historical regulations addressing intoxication and other threats to safe arms use. Reading Bruen’s “law-abiding, responsible citizens” language in a practical, institutionally workable way, Congress may impose categorical disqualifications on non-law-abiding persons when the disqualifying condition is cabined to current, regular unlawful use rather than remote or sporadic conduct. The Fifth Circuit’s as-applied approach would substantially disable a longstanding, frequently used federal public-safety statute and is not compelled by Bruen’s analogue inquiry, which tolerates modern regulations addressing persistent dangerousness even if they do not require proof of intoxication at the precise moment of possession.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 922(g)(3) regulates possession by persons who, by virtue of ongoing unlawful drug use or addiction, present a heightened risk of impaired judgment, and under Bruen the government need not identify a “historical twin” but a relevantly similar tradition addressing comparable dangers and burdens. Historical analogues—particularly longstanding restrictions on carrying or using arms while intoxicated and other status-linked limits aimed at preventing armed violence by those with impaired self-control—support a prohibition that targets a continuing condition rather than only the moment of visible intoxication. Hemani’s as-applied challenge would effectively recharacterize the statute as an intoxication-at-the-moment rule, but that is not what Congress enacted in 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), and Bruen does not require the Court to rewrite the text to save it. Giving due weight to Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework and the Court’s instruction to reason by analogy, § 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied to an active, habitual unlawful user without requiring proof of contemporaneous impairment at the instant of possession.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: As applied to Hemani, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) fits within Bruen’s requirement that modern regulations be justified by a “relevantly similar” historical analogue, not a historical “twin.” Historical tradition supports temporarily disarming individuals whose ongoing condition creates heightened risk—such as regulations targeting intoxication and other states associated with impaired judgment—even if the person is not proven intoxicated at the precise moment of possession, and Congress may operationalize that tradition through a contemporaneity/regular-use standard for “unlawful user.” Given the statute’s public-safety function and administrability, I would not constitutionalize an individualized, moment-of-possession intoxication finding that would severely undercut a core federal tool and produce arbitrary enforcement outcomes. Properly applied, § 922(g)(3) can be limited to active, habitual unlawful users with a temporal nexus to use, aligning with Bruen’s analogical framework while preserving procedural fairness.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Second Amendment allows Congress to disarm a person who is an “unlawful user of” controlled substances under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), even when the person is not shown to be intoxicated at the exact time of firearm possession, and specifically whether the statute is constitutional as applied to Ali Danial Hemani.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) (prohibiting firearm possession by anyone who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance”) and the Second Amendment to the U.S. Constitution (interpreted under the history-and-tradition framework from N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that § 922(g)(3) is consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation because history supports disarming categories of persons whose condition or ongoing conduct makes firearm possession especially dangerous (including those akin to intoxicated persons and others considered a heightened risk). The government emphasizes that the statute targets active, habitual unlawful drug users (not mere past use) and that courts upholding the law have found sufficiently analogous historical regulations. It further stresses that the Fifth Circuit’s invalidation of most applications of § 922(g)(3) creates (and deepens) a circuit conflict and threatens an important, frequently used federal public-safety statute affecting hundreds of prosecutions annually.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Hemani argues that § 922(g)(3), as applied, violates the Second Amendment under Bruen because the government cannot identify a well-established historical analogue from the Founding era that broadly disarmed people based on unlawful drug use—especially where the individual is not proved to be under the influence at the moment of possession. Respondent’s supporting amicus (Prof. Joel S. Johnson) also emphasizes that Bruen’s historical test has produced inconsistent outcomes and that courts struggle to identify representative analogues; on this view, the Fifth Circuit correctly concluded that the cited historical laws (e.g., temporary restrictions on carrying while intoxicated) are not analogous to a categorical ban keyed to “unlawful user” status.
key_precedents: N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen
United States v. Hill (E.D. Va. 2023), aff’d (4th Cir. 2025), cert. denied (2025)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s central objection—that the Government’s analogues (intoxication-at-the-moment, surety/affray) are conduct- and occasion-based and thus cannot justify a categorical, status-based disarmament—has real force, especially given Bruen’s demand for a comparable “why” and “how.” But Rahimi clarifies that we do not require a historical twin, and a narrowing construction (as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize) that reads “is an unlawful user” to mean contemporaneous, regular unlawful use tethers § 922(g)(3) to a time-limited, risk-based condition rather than a free-floating, permanent status disability. That approach directly answers Justice Gorsuch’s vagueness/lenity concerns by requiring a rigorous, close-in-time evidentiary showing, while avoiding the Fifth Circuit’s sweeping invalidation and preserving doctrinal stability under Heller’s and Bruen’s analogical method. On this record of active, habitual use, I would uphold the statute as applied and reserve harder marginal cases for another day.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposal to narrow “is an unlawful user” to contemporaneous, regular use does not supply the missing Founding-era analogue; it is an act of saving construction that effectively rewrites a criminal statute to fit modern policy concerns, contrary to text and the rule of lenity. Even as narrowed, § 922(g)(3) remains a categorical, status-based disarmament imposed without individualized process, unlike the surety and affray regimes Justice Kavanaugh invokes, which were triggered by specific threatening conduct or suspicion and typically allowed arms upon posting surety. Rahimi, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, recognizes that legislatures may address serious threats, but it upheld a scheme tied to a judicial finding and temporally limited order; it does not establish a Founding-era tradition for disarming ordinary citizens based on nonviolent, noncontemporaneous unlawful drug use. Under Bruen’s requirement of a well-established historical analogue with a comparable why and how, the Government’s analogues remain too episodic and process-bound to justify this broad prohibition as applied here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch have the strongest objection: Bruen requires a Founding-era analogue with comparable why/how, and the cited intoxication and surety regimes were typically event-driven and often process-laden, not a broad status ban. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively answer that the statute’s text—“is an unlawful user”—is best read to require a contemporaneous, ongoing pattern of unlawful use, which makes § 922(g)(3) a temporary, condition-linked restriction rather than a permanent disability; that narrowing also alleviates the lenity/vagueness concern. Rahimi matters because it confirms that our tradition tolerates disarmament of those posing a serious threat, and an ongoing, provable impairment-and-lawbreaking condition fits that dangerousness rationale even if historical mechanisms differed. On this record, the proper course is to uphold the statute as applied with a demanding contemporaneity requirement, not to invalidate an important public-safety tool based on marginal hypotheticals.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right to press that the cited intoxication and surety/affray laws were often occasion-based and sometimes process-laden, so they are not a Founding-era “twin” for a free-floating, permanent status ban. But under Bruen’s analogical inquiry—reinforced by Rahimi’s recognition that legislatures may disarm defined categories posing heightened risk—the relevant question is whether the tradition supports temporally limited disarmament keyed to a present, dangerous condition, and Chief Justice Roberts’s narrowing construction (reading “is an unlawful user” to require contemporaneous, regular use) supplies that tether and avoids the elastic status problem. Rahimi matters here even if it involved judicial findings, because it confirms that the Second Amendment tolerates preventive disarmament grounded in concrete, current risk rather than requiring the State to wait for violence, and § 922(g)(3) as applied to active, habitual use functions as a time-limited risk restriction. Given the real-world stakes for public safety and vulnerable communities, I would not constitutionalize the Fifth Circuit’s moment-of-intoxication demand, while leaving marginal, remote-use cases for as-applied challenges where the Government cannot show present regular use.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s best argument is that the Founding-era analogues (surety/going-armed, intoxication rules) were conduct- and occasion-based and often included individualized suspicion or process, so a categorical ban keyed to an “elastic” status risks exceeding the historical “how.” But Rahimi’s clarification—emphasized by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett—shifts the inquiry to whether the regulation is comparably justified and comparably tailored, not whether it replicates the same procedural mechanism, and the present-tense text “is an unlawful user” supports a narrowing construction requiring contemporaneous, regular unlawful use. That construction answers the overbreadth/vagueness concern by tethering disarmament to an ongoing risk condition (temporary in practical operation), bringing § 922(g)(3) closer to the historical pattern of time-limited restrictions for heightened danger even if the trigger differs from surety proceedings. Justice Thomas is right to insist we not substitute a free-floating “dangerousness” principle for history, but on a properly cabined reading of the statute, the Government’s analogues and Rahimi’s framework suffice to uphold the law as applied on evidence of active, habitual use near the time of possession.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s narrowing construction—that “is an unlawful user” means current, habitual use—addresses some vagueness and overbreadth concerns, but it still does not supply the Government’s burden under Bruen to identify a historical analogue with a comparable “how.” The cited intoxication-carry and surety/affray regimes were episodic, conduct- and occasion-based, and typically involved contemporaneous impairment, individualized suspicion, or judicial process; they do not justify an ongoing, categorical possession ban keyed to a status defined by an imprecise temporal line. Rahimi, as Justice Thomas emphasizes, upheld disarmament tied to a judicial finding and a time-limited order, and I do not read it to bless a free-floating “dangerousness” principle that lets Congress criminalize gun possession based on noncontemporaneous, nonviolent unlawful conduct without comparable historical process. Under a textualist and separation-of-powers lens, if Congress wants a narrower intoxication-at-possession rule or a process-based dangerousness regime, it must enact it clearly; we should not salvage an historically novel firearms disability by rewriting the statute through narrowing construction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Founding-era intoxication and surety/affray laws were typically event-triggered, temporary, and often process-based, so they are not a clean match for a categorical § 922(g)(3) ban keyed to “status.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the statutory present tense—“is an unlawful user”—supports a narrowing construction requiring contemporaneous, regular unlawful use close in time to possession, which makes the prohibition functionally temporary and risk-tethered rather than a permanent “bad person” disability. Under Bruen and Rahimi, the government need not produce a historical twin; it must show a relevant analogue with a comparable why and how, and a time-limited disarmament tied to an ongoing impairment-and-risk condition fits better than the Fifth Circuit’s moment-of-intoxication rule. Justice Gorsuch’s vagueness/lenity concern is real, but it argues for insisting on a rigorous contemporaneity showing in as-applied cases, not for invalidating the statute where the record demonstrates active, habitual use.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s central objection—that Founding-era intoxication and surety/affray laws were episodic, process-laden, and thus cannot justify a broad status-based disarmament—lands only if § 922(g)(3) is read as an untethered, permanent disability. Textually, however, the present-tense “is an unlawful user” is best construed, as Chief Justice Roberts urges, to require a current, ongoing pattern of unlawful use close in time to possession, which narrows the law’s “how” toward a temporary, condition-based restriction rather than a free-floating status ban. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity/vagueness concern strengthens that narrowing construction and demands a rigorous contemporaneity showing in as-applied cases, but it does not defeat the statute where the record demonstrates sustained use proximate to possession. Rahimi matters here because, as Justice Kagan notes, it confirms that our tradition allows disarmament keyed to present dangerousness; with a demanding “current-use” construction, this application fits that dangerousness analogue even absent proof of intoxication at the precise moment of possession.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best argument remains that the Government’s cited analogues were episodic, conduct- and process-linked restrictions, so a broad, status-based reading of § 922(g)(3) would be historically untethered and potentially indeterminate. But Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s narrowing construction—reading “is an unlawful user” to require a contemporaneous, regular pattern of unlawful use close in time to possession—substantially answers the mismatch by making the restriction temporary and risk-linked, more akin in “why” and “how” to historical measures addressing impaired or dangerous gun possession. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity/vagueness concerns reinforce (rather than defeat) that approach: they counsel insisting on rigorous proof of current, habitual use and leaving marginal, poorly supported prosecutions for as-applied challenges, not facial invalidation. Rahimi, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, supports focusing on danger-based, time-limited disarmament; the key is to demand procedural reliability in showing Hemani actually fell within that ongoing-risk category at the time of possession.

John Roberts.reasoning: As applied to Hemani, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) can be sustained on narrow grounds consistent with Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework because it targets an ongoing condition of unlawful, habitual drug use that bears on dangerousness, not mere past use, and it need not be limited to proof of intoxication at the precise moment of possession. Bruen reaffirmed that the Second Amendment protects law-abiding citizens and requires analogy rather than a historical “twin,” and historical practice supports disarming or restricting firearm access for persons whose status or conduct renders them especially dangerous (including restrictions tied to intoxication and other public-safety rationales). Upholding the statute in this limited, active-user application also respects institutional legitimacy and avoids the sweeping invalidation embraced by the Fifth Circuit, while leaving for another day any vagueness or overbreadth concerns at the margins of the “unlawful user” definition. This approach hews closely to precedent and preserves a significant, longstanding federal public-safety tool without expanding Second Amendment doctrine beyond what Bruen and Heller require.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text protects “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms,” and under Bruen the Government bears the burden to justify § 922(g)(3) by pointing to a well-established historical analogue from the Founding era with a similar “why” and “how.” The proffered analogues—temporary bans on carrying while intoxicated and other narrow, conduct-based restrictions—do not support a categorical, status-based prohibition on mere “unlawful user” status untethered to intoxication at the time of possession, as applied to Hemani. Because § 922(g)(3) disarms a class of persons based on ongoing unlawful conduct rather than adjudicated dangerousness and lacks a sufficiently analogous Founding-era tradition, it cannot stand under the history-and-tradition test. Precedent to the contrary should not be preserved where it conflicts with the Constitution’s original public meaning and Bruen’s methodological command.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 922(g)(3) is a permissible, status-based disarmament law because its text targets persons who are current “unlawful user[s]” of controlled substances, i.e., those engaged in ongoing illegal conduct that bears directly on public safety, not merely those with remote past use. Under Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework, the relevant analogue is the longstanding tradition of disarming persons deemed not “law-abiding, responsible citizens,” including regulations aimed at those whose condition or conduct creates an elevated risk of armed violence; Congress may address the comparable problem of impaired judgment and heightened dangerousness associated with habitual illegal drug use even if the individual is not proven intoxicated at the precise moment of possession. Reading Bruen to require a Founding-era twin for every modern risk-based category would hamstring legislatures confronting materially similar dangers with new modalities, and the practical consequences of invalidating § 922(g)(3) would substantially undermine a major federal public-safety tool used in numerous prosecutions. Because Hemani’s as-applied challenge seeks to exempt an active unlawful drug user from a targeted disarmament measure, I would uphold § 922(g)(3) as consistent with the Second Amendment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: As applied to an active, habitual “unlawful user” of controlled substances, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) is a constitutionally permissible firearm restriction consistent with the Second Amendment under Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework. History reflects a longstanding tradition of temporarily disarming or restricting arms for persons whose ongoing condition or conduct makes firearm possession especially dangerous—analogous to laws regulating the armed use of weapons by the intoxicated or otherwise presenting heightened risk—so Congress need not prove intoxication at the exact moment of possession to address the real and predictable danger tied to continual unlawful drug use. Rahimi confirms that the Second Amendment tolerates categorical disarmament when the government can identify relevant historical analogues aimed at preventing gun violence by those shown to pose a serious threat, and § 922(g)(3) serves that same preventive function for active unlawful users. Given the statute’s practical public-safety role and its focused application to current unlawful users (not mere past users), I would uphold it as applied to Hemani.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Bruen, the Government need not produce a “historical twin,” but must identify a relevant analogue with a similar “why” and “how.” Rahimi explains that our tradition permits disarming persons shown to pose a heightened risk of violence, and it treats surety/going-armed regimes as instructive because they addressed public-safety dangers through targeted limits rather than blanket bans. Section 922(g)(3) can fit that tradition when applied to a person who is a current, regular “unlawful user” whose ongoing drug use plausibly creates an enduring impairment-and-risk condition, even if intoxication is not proved at the precise moment of possession; read that way, the statute’s text (“is an unlawful user”) demands contemporaneity and avoids a purely status-based, permanent disarmament. As applied to Hemani, if the record shows sustained, ongoing unlawful use close in time to firearm possession (not remote or sporadic past use), the burden is met and the conviction may stand.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text covers Hemani’s possession of a firearm, so under Bruen the Government bears the burden to identify a representative historical analogue for disarming someone based on “unlawful user” status rather than contemporaneous intoxication. The proffered analogues—surety and affray regimes and scattered restrictions on carrying while intoxicated—regulated the manner or occasion of carry (and often required individualized suspicion), not a categorical, ongoing prohibition keyed to an imprecise status term like “is an unlawful user of” in 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3). Because the statute as applied here does not turn on being intoxicated at the time of possession and the historical record does not show a Founding-era tradition of disarming ordinary citizens for nonviolent, noncontemporaneous substance use, the Government has not carried its Bruen burden. Any ambiguity in extending criminal liability based on an elastic status concept should also be resolved narrowly, consistent with separation-of-powers principles and the rule of lenity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: As applied to an active, habitual “unlawful user,” 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) fits within the Second Amendment’s history-and-tradition framework because our tradition has long permitted temporarily disarming categories of persons whose ongoing condition makes firearm misuse especially dangerous, not solely those shown intoxicated at the precise moment of possession. Heller’s assurance that “longstanding prohibitions” on possession by felons and the mentally ill are “presumptively lawful,” reiterated in McDonald and echoed in my Bruen concurrence, supports Congress’s ability to impose status-based limits on firearm possession for groups posing heightened risk. Rahimi likewise recognizes a tradition of temporary disarmament of dangerous persons and allows categorical approaches where the category tracks historically recognized danger. The Fifth Circuit’s narrower requirement of contemporaneous intoxication reads the tradition too tightly and would undermine a workable, important public-safety statute aimed at present, ongoing unlawful drug use rather than past conduct.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Bruen, the Government must show that § 922(g)(3)’s restriction is consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, not that the Founding had a precise twin for modern drug laws. As Rahimi illustrates, legislatures historically could disarm individuals whose ongoing condition or adjudicated status made gun possession especially dangerous, and a contemporaneous “unlawful user” restriction is analogous in purpose and burden to historical regulations addressing intoxication and other risk-based limitations. Textually, § 922(g)(3) targets those who “is an unlawful user of” controlled substances—i.e., current, regular unlawful use—so an as-applied challenge fails where the record shows ongoing unlawful use even if intoxication at the exact moment of possession is not proved. Respecting precedent’s methodological consistency, I would uphold the statute as applied to Hemani because it fits within Bruen’s and Rahimi’s history-and-tradition framework permitting disarmament of persons posing a heightened risk to public safety.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework as clarified in United States v. Rahimi (2024), § 922(g)(3) fits within a historical tradition of temporarily disarming persons whose ongoing condition or conduct makes firearm possession especially dangerous, even if the person is not proven intoxicated at the precise moment of possession. The statute is not a sweeping ban on a disfavored class; it is cabined to those who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to” controlled substances, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), a status that (properly proved) reflects current, repeated unlawful use and heightened risk—an analogy sufficiently close to historical restrictions on carrying while intoxicated and other danger-based disarmament practices. From a procedural-fairness perspective, constitutionality as applied to Hemani depends on a rigorous showing that he was an “unlawful user” in a contemporaneous, ongoing sense (not merely a past user), but where that showing is made, the practical public-safety consequences support upholding the law under Rahimi’s dangerousness principle. Accordingly, I would reverse the Fifth Circuit’s broad invalidation and uphold § 922(g)(3) at least as applied on a record demonstrating active, habitual use contemporaneous with possession.
